analysis.one_liner: Eliminates tuition and fees at community colleges and public four-year colleges for most students.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee, dying without a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The College for All Act would create a federal-state partnership that pays states and tribal colleges to wipe out tuition and required fees for every student at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, and for working- and middle-class students — roughly those with household income up to $125,000, or $250,000 for married couples — at public four-year colleges. It would fund private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions to do the same. It also raises the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790, lets Pell money cover living expenses, extends how long students can use it, and extends Pell eligibility to Dreamer students and others with temporary immigration status. The bill was introduced in June 2023, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and their families. Community college students of any income level would pay no tuition or required fees. Students at public four-year colleges from households earning up to $125,000 (or up to $250,000 for married couples) would pay no tuition or fees. Pell recipients would get larger awards — up to $14,790 at participating schools — more years to use them, and the ability to spend the money on rent and living costs, not just tuition. Dreamer students and students with temporary protected status would become newly eligible for federal aid. Historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions would receive large new federal funding, and adjunct faculty would gain from a requirement that states move most instruction to tenured or tenure-track jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community college and public college students

how_it_helps.text: Funds a federal-state partnership to eliminate tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, and for students with household income up to $125,000 (single) or $250,000 (married) at public four-year institutions [S2] [S3].

Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790, extends the period students can use Pell Grants to 7.5 years, allows the money to cover living and non-tuition expenses, and expands eligibility to Dreamer students and those with DACA or temporary protected status [S2] [S3].
Provides grants so private nonprofit historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions can eliminate tuition and fees for eligible students [S2] [S3].

Requires participating states to maintain per-student funding at or above recent averages, cap out-of-state tuition at marginal cost, move toward 75 percent of instruction by tenured or tenure-track faculty, and improve transfer of community college credits to four-year degrees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations — the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2033 with no stated dollar cap — and state taxpayers, who must eventually cover 20 percent of the program cost and maintain their own higher education spending at or above recent averages as a condition of receiving federal money.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes unlimited spending — 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2024 through 2033 — without a stated total cost, and appropriates money directly rather than waiting for annual budget review [S3].

Free tuition would also cover students from households earning up to $250,000 for married couples, meaning some well-off families who can pay would get free tuition alongside lower-income students [S3].
States must eventually pay 20 percent of the cost and must keep their own higher education funding at or above recent three-year averages to receive federal money, which pressures state budgets [S3].
Eligibility rules would extend to students regardless of immigration status, including Dreamers, a provision that was certain to draw strong opposition and raise the bill's political cost [S3].

Participating states must meet federal conditions on faculty tenure-track ratios, transfer agreements, and instruction spending, which would trade money for state control over how public colleges are run [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and concrete: families with incomes up to $125,000–$250,000 could save thousands of dollars a year in tuition, and the largest cost groups — community college students and Pell recipients — get the most help. The honest cost objection is that the bill writes a blank check: it appropriates whatever is necessary for a decade with no stated price, and would require federal money to flow through state budget systems with strings attached. Whether that trade is worth it depends on judgments the record in this bill file does not resolve, because the Congressional Budget Office never scored the bill and no committee ever examined it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the College for All Act on June 14, 2023, with nine Democratic senators joining as original cosponsors: Blumenthal, Padilla, Murphy, Welch, Warren, Markey, Van Hollen, and Merkley [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].

The committee took no further action; the bill's complete action history ends with the referral, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].
Total cosponsorship reached 10 senators, all Democrats; no Republican supported the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No student's tuition went down. The bill's failure leaves the status quo intact: states and families keep paying current tuition, private lenders keep making student loans, and for-profit colleges keep competing for students without facing a free public alternative. It also spared taxpayers from an uncapped federal spending commitment whose cost was never scored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: lenders, for-profit colleges, and taxpayers

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized nine Democratic cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Tammy Blumenthal, Alex Padilla, Chris Murphy, Peter Welch, Elizabeth Warren, Ed Markey, Chris Van Hollen, Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a 10-sponsor bloc.

for.what_they_did: Brought total cosponsorship to 10, all Democrats.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no action for the remainder of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 118th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's 10 cosponsors was a Republican, and the bill faced large-scale federal spending and immigration provisions that Republican senators opposed; the measure never advanced to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats, the sponsor is an independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican ever signed on or acted to move the bill; the record shows no cross-party support [S4].

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and servicers
industries.note: Free tuition and larger Pell Grants would shrink the amount students must borrow, reducing the pool of loans on which lenders collect interest and fees for years after graduation. The bill's defeat preserves that borrowing market.

The bill excludes proprietary institutions from the tuition-elimination partnership and bars states from counting for-profit college spending toward state support, while creating a free public alternative that would pull students away. Its death keeps for-profit colleges competing on equal footing.

Only private nonprofit historically Black and minority-serving institutions could get tuition-elimination grants; other private colleges would not, and a free public option would pressure their enrollment. The bill never advanced, so they faced no change.

industries.industry: Historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: These institutions would receive direct federal funding to eliminate tuition, a major new revenue stream that also lowers costs for their students. The bill's death left them dependent on existing funding.

The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2033 with no stated cap, an open-ended federal commitment. Its failure spares taxpayers that cost while leaving families to keep paying tuition.
